drills.q: State the full IAM policy evaluation order from first check to last.
drills.a: Explicit deny anywhere > SCP > RCP > resource-based policy > permissions boundary > session policy > identity-based policy > default deny.

drills.q: A role's identity policy grants s3:*. It still can't touch a bucket. Name three possible ceiling-layer causes.
drills.a: An SCP not explicitly allowing s3 actions at the OU/account level; an RCP restricting the resource side; a permissions boundary attached to the role that excludes S3. Any one of these caps the identity policy regardless of how permissive it looks.

drills.q: Why doesn't a resource policy alone satisfy a cross-account access request the way it does for same-account access?
drills.a: Cross-account access requires both sides to explicitly allow: the resource policy on the owning account's side, AND the identity policy on the calling account's principal. Same-account grants can rely on the resource policy alone since the identity is already inside the trust boundary being evaluated by that resource.

drills.q: Explain the confused deputy problem and how sts:ExternalId fixes it.
drills.a: A third-party vendor with AssumeRole access into many customers' accounts could be tricked or buggy in a way that acts on the wrong customer's account, since role ARNs can look similar or be stored incorrectly. ExternalId is a per-customer secret placed in the trust policy condition that the vendor must include on every AssumeRole call for that specific customer, so a mismatched or missing ExternalId fails the assumption instead of silently succeeding against the wrong tenant.

drills.q: Why is iam:PassRole considered a privilege-escalation path rather than a benign permission?
drills.a: PassRole lets a principal attach a role to a service resource (like a Lambda function) without being granted that role's permissions directly. If the principal can also create the resource type that accepts the role (e.g., create a Lambda), they can run code under that role's full permission set, effectively escalating to whatever the passed role can do.

drills.q: Contrast aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount with a concrete scenario for each.
drills.a: aws:SourceArn: 'only my exact SNS topic ARN may invoke this Lambda' — single-resource, strongest confused-deputy defense. aws:SourceAccount: 'any S3 bucket in account X may trigger this' — trusts the whole account when the exact resource ARN isn't fixed ahead of time.

drills.q: What's the mechanical difference between IRSA and EKS Pod Identity for granting a pod AWS credentials?
drills.a: IRSA: per-cluster OIDC provider registered with IAM, role's trust policy references that OIDC issuer and a specific service-account subject, a mutating webhook injects a projected token into the pod. Pod Identity: an EKS Auth API association plus a Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet on each node fetch credentials on the pod's behalf, with the trust relationship managed by EKS itself rather than the role's own trust policy, making the role portable across clusters.

drills.q: What gap in SCP coverage did Resource Control Policies (RCPs, GA November 2024) close?
drills.a: SCPs only restrict identity policies of principals within the org, so they can't stop an in-org identity from writing a resource policy that grants access to a principal OUTSIDE the org. RCPs act as a ceiling on the resource-policy side directly, capping what any resource policy can grant regardless of which identity authored it.

drills.q: What are permissions boundaries designed to enable operationally, beyond just 'restricting a role'?
drills.a: Delegated IAM administration — letting app teams self-service create their own roles and policies (often via CI/Terraform) while a mandatory boundary caps the maximum they can ever grant themselves, so central security reviews the boundary policy once instead of every team's individual role definitions.

drills.q: You're debugging an unexpected AccessDenied. What's the first command you run and why?
drills.a: aws sts get-caller-identity, to confirm which principal is actually making the call. Using the wrong CLI profile or an unexpectedly still-assumed role is the most common self-inflicted cause of a denial that looks inexplicable given the policy you think applies.

drills.q: What does IAM Access Analyzer's 'unused access' feature actually measure, and what's its blind spot?
drills.a: It measures permissions not exercised in observed CloudTrail activity over a lookback window and flags them as removal candidates. Its blind spot: legitimate but rarely-used permissions (annual DR runbooks) get flagged as false positives, and it cannot distinguish a permission used once legitimately from one used once maliciously.
